packetScope: Four distinct inspected works: two renewed Arapaho Project resources, one separate published grammar excerpt and one collaborative research article. Related online grammar/lesson pages count as a single learning collection.

sources.title: History of the Northern Arapaho Tribe
sources.publisher: The Arapaho Project / University of Colorado Boulder
sources.annotation: A substantive Northern-focused history connects changing Plains relationships, dispossession and educational institutions. The undated page is useful for historical orientation; its contemporary assessments, estimates and broad generalizations are not current measurements or substitutes for tribal accounts.
sources.contentReviewScope: Full actual narrative read: pre-contact, nineteenth-century, early reservation and contemporary-era sections. Synthesis selects river-valley distinctions, 1878 Wind River settlement, assimilation pressures and later educational renewal.
sources.publicationDate: Undated page; copyright and crawl dates do not establish publication

sources.publisher: The Arapaho Project / University of Colorado Boulder
sources.annotation: One learning collection offers a substantive grammar introduction alongside navigation to educational resources. Selected text explains word structure and grammatical categories. The undated landing page’s speaker estimates are excluded; linked media, dictionaries and narrative contents are not thereby inspected.
sources.contentReviewScope: Actual language and grammar page bodies read; lesson page reviewed as navigation only. Count the related pages once. No audio listening, complete curriculum, dictionary or narrative review.

sources.title: Northern Arapaho virtual reality linguistic elicitation
sources.author: Phineas Kelly and Andrew Cowell
sources.publisher: Language Documentation and Description; author-deposited version in NSF Public Access Repository
sources.annotation: A research article describes an elicitation method developed with Northern Arapaho elders and educators. It concerns documentation, rather than demonstrated classroom effectiveness. The deposited reading copy has placeholder citation fields; the work’s publication date was independently checked through the journal’s university announcement.
sources.contentReviewScope: Actual 13-page deposited PDF: title, selected introduction/background and method on 2–5, conclusion/acknowledgements on 10. No audio/video, application testing, underlying archive or detailed statistical reanalysis.
sources.publicationDate: 2023-05-26 publication, confirmed by University of Virginia’s journal announcement; deposited copy identifies 2023

claimBlocks.text: The Arapaho Project’s Northern Arapaho history distinguishes northern communities centered on the North Platte from southern communities associated with the Arkansas valley. It places the Northern Arapaho move to Wind River in 1878. Its account also connects boarding schools, allotment and pressures on language with later community-controlled education and cultural renewal. This is a Northern-focused historical synthesis; its undated descriptions of contemporary conditions require fresh corroboration.
claimBlocks.sourceLocator: Nineteenth Century, Early Reservation Era and Contemporary Era; actual page lines 24–39

claimBlocks.text: The Arapaho Project explains that words can combine many meaningful elements. Verbs can express information that English distributes across several words, including participants, tense and aspect. Its animate/inanimate distinctions are grammatical, rather than a simple division between living and nonliving things. These introductory explanations offer a starting point for exploring language structure; the linked collection should be used with community teaching and does not certify proficiency.
claimBlocks.sourceLocator: Grammar: introductory explanation, Verb Categories, Verb Modifications and Nouns

claimBlocks.suggestedSection: A grammar grounded in documented usage
claimBlocks.text: Cowell and Arapaho coauthor Alonzo Moss, Sr. present their grammar through communicative use as well as forms and rules. Its introduction explains a corpus combining historical records, educational materials and more recent speech, with sources from Wyoming and Oklahoma. The authors identify revisions and corrections to earlier transcriptions. This makes the book useful for understanding how linguistic knowledge is documented, while its evidence remains distinct from a current speaker census.
claimBlocks.sourceLocator: Printed 4–7 / excerpt PDF 11–14, especially aims, source list and corpus discussion

claimBlocks.text: Kelly and Cowell describe virtual-reality language documentation developed through iterative work with the Northern Arapaho Language and Culture Commission. Elders helped select contexts, and applications were checked for usability and cultural appropriateness. Sessions in 2019–2020 informed the study. The authors compare elicited language with other documentation methods; their findings concern recorded speech and research design, rather than proof that an application produces fluent learners.

inspections.method: Fresh actual-page reading of all narrative sections beyond the title and navigation.
evidence: Actual nineteenth-century section differentiates North Platte and Arkansas valley associations and gives the Northern move to Wind River in 1878.
Early reservation and contemporary-era sections describe boarding/mission schools, allotment, later community-controlled schools, and language/culture work.
inspections.limits: Exclude speculative ancient frozen-river identification, undated numbers/ages, current living-speaker assertions about related peoples, sweeping ceremony/cultural-loss judgments, current unemployment or program-status claims. The page’s treaty phrasing should not be relied on for legal ratification conclusions; actual treaties are outside this packet.

inspections.method: Fresh actual language/grammar text reading; lesson page’s topic list inspected but no substantive lessons embedded there. Grammar page provides enough original explanatory content for a substantive selected collection.
evidence: Grammar introduction explains morphemes and complex words; Verb Categories distinguishes transitivity and grammatical animacy.
Nouns explicitly says grammatical animacy cannot simply be predicted from real-life properties.
inspections.limits: No audio playback, pronunciation assessment, story/narrative reading, full dictionary/curriculum review or current vitality claim. The landing page’s general historical assertions about other Algonquian peoples and early printing are not adopted. The broken language-evolution link remains unread.

inspections.method: Actual public publisher PDF rendered as 19 pages by web reader; substantive introduction 1–7 read, beyond contents and catalogue. Separate local download returned 403, so no local PDF is claimed. The normal web reader supplied the actual text.
evidence: Printed 4 states the reference grammar’s functional/pragmatic aims and attention to communicative choices.
Printed 5–7 identifies text, curricular and recording sources, field notes and Moss’s contributions; material from both Wyoming and Oklahoma is identified.
Printed 5 discusses corrections/improvements in glosses; sources and communicative evidence are explicitly differentiated.
inspections.limits: Do not describe the selected excerpt as a complete 544-page grammar review or count the same book’s later edition separately. Underlying corpus materials are not independently inspected and provide no permission for republishing narratives, songs, names or recordings. No present demographic/competence estimate or negative generalization about Southern or Northern learners is adopted.

bibliographicSupport.scope: Actual publisher metadata gives authors, original publication year 2008, 544 pages and the linked excerpt. Metadata supports bibliography, not an extra counted work.

inspections.method: NSF web reader initially returned 502; ordinary public HTTPS download succeeded (1,729,289 bytes; 13 pages). Actual selected pages extracted and read. The deposited first page cites 2023 but has X(X) placeholders; the university journal announcement independently confirms date/title/authors.
evidence: Page 3 dates elicitation sessions to 2019–2020; methodological collaboration is distinct from current program delivery.
Page 5 explicitly describes iterative development with the Commission, checking usability and cultural appropriateness, and elder selection of contexts.
Page 10 frames comparison in terms of the linguistic data elicited; it does not report a controlled learner-fluency outcome.
inspections.limits: No sacred narrative wording, exact sensitive places, models, drone images, portraits, maps, interviews or personal health information reproduced. Do not generalize to all Arapaho governments or Southern programs. No 2023 speaker total is presented as current. Reading the paper does not mean listening to recordings or independently testing the applications/statistics.

bibliographicSupport.scope: Actual university announcement lists this article, authors and 2023-05-26 publication. Its own announcement date is 2024-02-16, not the article date. Not a separate source count.

groupingAndIntegrationNotes: Renew p18-s5 and p18-s6 in place, preserving stable IDs. Do not append duplicate cards or count the two renewals as new additions.

Keep the brief online learning collection as one work. The separate 2008 reference grammar is counted once through substantive original introductory pages; catalogue, excerpt and a later edition are not additional works.

Replace or revise the legacy p18-s5/p18-s6 body sections rather than append this packet blindly. Recalculate derived totals across overview and all retained prose; the source-specific ceilings below assume only the supplied claim blocks.

Northern Arapaho Tribe, Southern Arapaho within the Cheyenne and Arapaho Tribes, Eastern Shoshone and Gros Ventre/Aaniiih require distinct identities. Shared reservation, language-family relationships or a jointly named government do not make these peoples equivalent.
No audio, source media, narratives or underlying corpora are republished. The linked academic works are educational reading paths, not permission to reuse all associated cultural materials.
